extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism, mass communication, and media studies; journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and production standards that govern news content: routines, ethical norms, gatekeeping practices, and news values that shape what becomes news and how it's presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in ethical attitudes between newspaper editors and television news directors (SPJ survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some differences were discovered in the SPJ survey (Gersh, 1992b): television news producers were less likely to believe that it is ethical to change quotes; that having an effective code of ethics will enhance a news operation's credibility; that it is acceptable to report names and addresses of crime victims; and that it is acceptable to report about a criminal who had threatened to commit suicide if the story ran. Conversely, television news producers were more likely to approve source confidentiality; allow staffers to accept leadership positions in civic groups; judge stories newsworthy because of graphics and packaging; cooperate with an FBI request to embargo news about a kidnapping; include the name of press agents when their releases appear almost verbatim; and substantiate press releases before airing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list to compare ethical stances across media types; it identifies specific practices television producers are comparatively more or less likely to endorse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' approval of ethically questionable reporting practices (Weaver & Wilhoit survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey findings: only 5% saw any justification for divulging a confidential source; 20% approved claiming to be someone else to get a story; just over one-fourth approved paying people for confidential information or using personal documents without permission; around half thought badgering unwilling informants or using confidential business or government documents without authorization are justified; about two-thirds accepted going undercover as an employee to gain inside information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These percentages indicate which ethically controversial tactics have some professional acceptance and how acceptance varies by age and organizational size (older journalists less likely to approve; large organizations more likely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of professional role self-definition on content
rubrics_metrics.description: How journalists define their jobs affects the content they produce: journalists who see themselves as disseminators/neutrals write different accounts than interpreters/participants. Starck and Soloski (1977) found students who saw themselves as neutrals wrote the least fair and comprehensive stories; those midway between neutral and participant wrote the most objective and accurate stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a journalist's self-conception (neutral vs participant) to predict tendencies in fairness, comprehensiveness, and objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical standards can clash with other values
rubrics_metrics.description: Breed (1964) noted ethical standards can clash with values such as public decency, respect for convention, and orderliness; 'Accurate reporting is sometimes sacrificed to these other virtues of respect, decency, and order.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize trade-offs where accuracy may be subordinated to other social values; evaluate decisions in context of competing values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect influence of communicators' characteristics via attitudes and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicators' characteristics, backgrounds, and experiences do not directly determine media content; rather, they influence personal and professional attitudes and roles, of which professional roles and ethics have more influence on content than personal attitudes, values, and beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing content effects, trace influences through role/ethical frameworks rather than assuming direct translation from demographics or background to output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines as patterned constraints shaping content and gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines are patterned, routinized, repeated practices and forms media workers use to do their jobs; they form immediate context and constraints (e.g., gatekeepers winnow many potential messages to a few), producing standardized, recurring patterns of news and entertainment content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat routines as cohesive rules that become part of professional identity and that limit individual discretion; examine how routine practices determine selection and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television news 'news factory' routinization
rubrics_metrics.description: Television news often resembles a 'news factory' with routinization driven by frequent personnel turnover, complex technology requiring specialized roles, and consultants prescribing formulaic guidelines; results emphasize 'technically uniform, visually sophisticated, easy to understand, fast-paced, people-oriented stories that are produced in a minimum amount of time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect TV news to prioritize speed, visual appeal, and formula over depth; evaluate stories for those production-driven constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines make news and can distort social reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines allow everyday occurrences to be recognized and reconstituted as news (Tuchman); organizational and mundane features of news work promote a way of looking at events which can fundamentally distort them (Altheide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the existence and form of news often result from routinized recognition and framing processes rather than an objective 'event out there.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of routines: audience, organization, and suppliers (triangle model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media routines stem from constraints related to three stages: What is acceptable to the consumer (audience)? What is the organization capable of processing? What raw product is available from suppliers (sources)? Each routine fits somewhere in the triangle formed by these three stages and may serve one or more needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate any routine by locating which of the three constraints it primarily responds to; e.g., inverted pyramid serves both audience (readers can stop early) and organization (editors can trim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid routine (audience & organization needs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverted pyramid presents facts in order of decreasing importance so readers get the most important information early and editors can trim from the bottom up to fit available space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an example of a routine that balances audience attention constraints and organizational space/production needs; recognize the structural trade-offs it creates in storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values as yardsticks of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: News values distill what people find interesting and important; the text lists: (1) Prominence/importance (impact/how many lives it affects), (2) Human interest (celebrities, personal drama), (3) Conflict/controversy (signals important issues), (4) The unusual, (5) Timeliness (what's happening now), (6) Proximity (events near are more newsworthy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these values as conventional criteria guiding gatekeeper selection decisions; they predict audience appeal and direct consistent story selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity as a defensive routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity functions as a set of procedures serving a defensive function—protecting journalists and organizations from attack and legitimating media power—rather than solely as a core belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating objectivity, look for its ritualized procedures and organizational purposes (credibility protection, common style for syndication) rather than only normative claims about neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity procedures (attribution, verifiable facts, quotation, multiple names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity procedures include relying on verifiable facts, setting statements off in quotation marks, including many names in a story to keep the reporter's views out, presenting supplementary evidence for a 'fact,' and attributing statements to sources to protect against accusations of manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess news pieces for adherence to these procedures as signals of conformity to the objectivity routine; note that following these procedures can still produce distortions if important contrary information is omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity routine leads to omission of mobilizing information
rubrics_metrics.description: The objectivity routine often leads to omitting mobilizing information (instructions on what to do, where to go), especially if such information is negative, controversial, nonlocal, or in main/news/editorial sections, to avoid accusations of partisanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for absence of practical, mobilizing details in coverage as a possible consequence of objectivity-driven fear of partisanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure routine: narrative attributes applied to news
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevailing routine is to 'tell stories'—news stories are expected to display attributes of fiction and drama (structure and conflict, problem and denouement, rising and falling action, a beginning, a middle and an end) so they have inherent appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how narrative demands (clear plot lines, villains/heroes) shape selection and framing; beware that imposing narrative form can distort complex realities (e.g., melodramatic framing of the Iranian hostage crisis).

rubrics_metrics.name: News values as post hoc rationalizations and limits of audience-driven explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: News values were derived from analyzing actual news content and often serve as post hoc explanations that rationalize selections already made; audience may figure less prominently in routines than assumed (Project Censored examples of underreported important stories illustrate this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using news values to explain coverage, consider that they may rationalize prior organizational/routine choices and that important stories can be overlooked despite meeting news-value criteria.
